title: Vietnam
hook: where Theravada and Mahayana meet, and Chan becomes Thien

segments.voice: Yesterday, walking Borobudur: up through walls of story and out onto the plain terraces. Your line was from carvings to open sky. Did you find one open view when your head got crowded? Day eight hundred ninety-two.

Two temples, one country. In the Mekong Delta, in the far south of Vietnam, monks in saffron robes chant in Pali under steep, gilded Khmer roofs. A long way north, in a pagoda near Hanoi, a nun in brown robes sits in silent meditation, and an hour later the same hall fills with lay people chanting the name of Amitabha Buddha, a Mahayana practice. Same country. Same Buddha. Different robes, different languages, different streams of the teaching. Across Southeast Asia we've met both streams in stone: Theravada in Sri Lanka, Myanmar and Thailand, Mahayana at Angkor and Borobudur. In Vietnam, they live side by side today. Today, a country where two streams meet.
screen: `SAFFRON ROBES IN THE MEKONG DELTA.` → `BROWN ROBES NEAR HANOI.` → `ONE COUNTRY, TWO STREAMS.`

segments.voice: First, the two streams. Mahayana Buddhism came into Vietnam with texts written in Chinese characters, and it shaped pagodas and monasteries across the country. Theravada lives on too, especially among the Khmer communities of the south, with Pali chanting and saffron robes, and some Vietnamese monasteries follow it as well. Second, Chan becomes Thien. One Mahayana school, called Chan in China and Zen in Japan, is called Thien in Vietnam. Its heart is meditation: sitting, seeing clearly, not relying on words alone. Tradition says the name of all three comes from the old Indian word for meditation, dhyana. Third, a king on a mountain. Vietnamese tradition remembers a king named Tran Nhan Tong, who gave up his throne, became a monk, and went to live on Yen Tu mountain. The Thien school linked to him is called Truc Lam, the Bamboo Grove, and it's still practiced today. Fourth, both in one hall. In Vietnamese pagodas, Thien meditation and Pure Land chanting live side by side, sometimes on the same day, with the same people. People there don't treat it as a choice they must make. And beneath both streams is shared ground. The Dhammapada, in Max Müller's translation, puts it in one line: "Not to commit any sin, to do good, and to purify one's mind, that is the teaching of (all) the Awakened." A Khmer monk in the delta and a Thien nun near Hanoi could both say that line and mean it. Two streams, meeting, without one swallowing the other.
screen: `MAHAYANA AND THERAVADA, BOTH AT HOME.` · `CHAN IN CHINA, THIEN IN VIETNAM.` · `A KING WHO BECAME A MONK.` · `MEDITATION AND CHANTING, ONE HALL.` · then, large: `TWO STREAMS MEET.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice one meeting of two ways. Settle and breathe. Think of a place in your own life where two ways live together. Two languages in one kitchen. Two family traditions at one holiday table. A morning person and a night owl under one roof. Picture it clearly. Notice where the two rub against each other, and where they've quietly made room. You don't need to judge which way is right. Just let both be there, side by side, like the two streams. The bell holds the time.
Vietnam. A country where Mahayana and Theravada both make their home, and where the meditation school called Chan in China is called Thien. Today's word.
Your line: two streams meet. Today, when two ways of doing something collide near you, look for the place where they already make room for each other. Day eight hundred ninety-two.

howItsDone: In Vietnamese pagodas, monks, nuns and lay Buddhists practice Thien meditation and also chant the name of Amitabha Buddha, while Khmer Theravada temples in the south keep Pali chanting and the morning alms.

fork.setup: you're a lay Buddhist at a pagoda near Hanoi. the morning has silent Thien meditation; the evening has chanting of Amitabha's name. what do people there do?

notes: Dhammapada 183 quoted from Max Müller (1881); confirm exact wording, including the parenthetical '(all)'.
'Mahayana ... shaped pagodas and monasteries across the country': confirm.
Tran Nhan Tong, his abdication, life on Yen Tu and the Truc Lam school are presented as 'Vietnamese tradition remembers'; confirm.
The derivation of Chan / Thien / Zen from dhyana is given only as 'tradition says' under the claims rule; it is the standard account. Confirm.
'Some Vietnamese monasteries follow [Theravada] as well' (the Vietnamese Theravada / Nam tong communities): confirm.
The verse is used as shared ground without ranking either stream; Keeper should confirm it is fair to both.
